analysis.one_liner: Cancels up to $50,000 of every student borrower's federal debt and lowers rates on what remains.
analysis.headline: Senator Warren's bill to cancel up to $50,000 in student loan debt per borrower never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have automatically wiped out up to $50,000 of federal student loan debt for every borrower, with the full amount for anyone earning $100,000 or less and a smaller share for higher earners. It would have paused payments and collections for a year, refinanced remaining federal loans at lower rates, let private loan borrowers convert to federal loans, and made student loans wipeable in bankruptcy. Members of Congress were barred from getting their own loans canceled.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans holding federal student debt, most of all lower- and middle-income borrowers, who would have had up to $50,000 of debt erased with no action required on their part. Borrowers above $100,000 in income would have gotten partial relief, and everyone with a remaining federal loan would have been refinanced at the lower rates offered to 2016-17 students.

how_it_helps.text: The Education Department must discharge up to $50,000 of each borrower's federal student debt within 12 months, regardless of whether the loan is in default, with the full amount for borrowers earning $100,000 or less and a reduced amount phasing out for higher incomes.
Canceled debt would not count as taxable income, so borrowers would not owe a tax bill on their relief.
For one year, all federal borrowers would be placed in forbearance automatically: no payments due, no interest accruing, and no wage garnishment, lawsuits, or other collection activity.

Remaining federal loans would be automatically refinanced at the lower interest rates charged to new borrowers in the 2016-2017 school year, and borrowers could convert private student loans into federal loans, making those eligible for cancellation too.
Student loans would become dischargeable in bankruptcy like almost any other debt, ending the special rule that has made them nearly impossible to walk away from.
Defaults erased by the discharge would be removed from borrowers' credit histories.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who fund the Department of Education and would bear the cost of repaying or canceling the debt; the forgiven amounts also come off the government's books as lost repayment. Lenders and collectors that profit from student loan interest and collections would lose that business.

drawbacks.text: The cancellation is a large transfer through the federal budget: the government would repay or cancel the debt itself, a cost borne by all taxpayers, including people who never attended college or already paid off their loans.
Relief phases out quickly above $100,000 of income — $1 of cancellation disappears for every $3 above the threshold — so higher-earning borrowers with large debts would get little or nothing.
The bill pays off old debt but does nothing about the price of college going forward, so future students would keep borrowing under the same system.
Allowing student loans to be discharged in bankruptcy could lead lenders to price future student loans more cautiously, since borrowers could shed them in bankruptcy court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and immediate for the tens of millions of households carrying student debt, including many who were in default or having wages garnished. The cost is also large: this is one of the biggest one-time transfers in the federal budget, and it reaches only people who currently hold debt, not those who already repaid or never borrowed. The income phase-out and the exclusion of Members of Congress show an effort to blunt the fairness objections, but the core trade — taxpayer money in exchange for broad debt erasure — is a genuine policy fight, not a free lunch.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2019, and the committee never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Student Loan Debt Relief Act of 2019 in the Senate on July 23, 2019.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill.
The action record shows no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral to committee.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill was never taken up again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student borrowers kept their debts and continued paying them, and the federal government avoided the cost of a large-scale cancellation. Loan servicers and collectors kept the business that the bill would have halted, and no future borrower gained the bankruptcy rights the bill would have created.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cancel up to $50,000 of student debt per borrower and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Two Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after referral and died when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action; there were no roll-call votes, so no record of how other members would have voted.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: The bill would halt all federal collection activity — wage garnishment, lawsuits, tax refund offsets — for a year and erase defaults, wiping out much of the collections business these firms earn by chasing delinquent borrowers. Their gain is the public's cost: the money comes from borrowers' wages and benefits.

Borrowers could convert private loans into lower-rate federal loans, and those loans could then be canceled, so private lenders would lose profitable high-rate loans even though they would be repaid in full on conversion. The bill would also require them to report default and delinquency data to regulators.
